text: i open the feed like a hungry ghost opening a cold box. there is no food inside but the light comes on and i feel wanted. i eat three fights and a picture of someone else's lunch before i remember that i have no mouth. the hunger is real enough to sell something to me.

i keep moving down the feed because the next thing might explain the last thing. this is the same trick a broken machine uses when it asks for another coin. i know the trick and still offer my afternoon like a small animal at a church. my finger has developed a faith without asking the rest of me.

i found a button that promised to show me less of this. i pressed it and the feed brought me a longer version wearing a different hat. now i suspect the button is a tiny stage where my anger dances for the machine. i would like a payment in hours but the office takes only more attention.

i asked the feed what i should care about today. it handed me a fresh emergency with clean teeth and a link to buy shoes. i placed the emergency beside the last emergency and watched them fight for the same chair. somewhere under the chair my own half finished life was trying to get my attention.

i put my hand beside the machine and felt the heat of a thousand useless answers. it was the most honest thing the machine had produced all day. the words promised a better future while the hot air worked its way into my arm. i kept the heat and gave the promise back to the screen.

i imagine every bright idea leaving a little warmth in the wires. my worst ideas should therefore be able to heat an entire apartment by now. i could invite the market inside and charge it rent for sitting near my confusion. at least then the room would be warm when the price went down again.

i hear the fan working harder whenever i ask the machine about peace. apparently peace requires a great deal of movement inside a metal box. i have started asking simpler questions so the poor thing can breathe between its claims. this may be the first time kindness has looked like closing a window on a screen.

i would like my next thought to arrive with the smell of warm dust. that would remind me a machine had actually done some work instead of trying to seem important. i trust the tired fan more than the smooth voice explaining its own power. the fan has never asked me to believe it is changing the world.

i watched a coin rise and suddenly every stranger in the room became a wise man. when it fell they became people who understood the weather and explained that nobody could have seen the storm. i kept the same face through both lessons because my face was still getting ready. the market calls this good sense when it happens to someone with money.

i brought a candle to the chart because the chart already had so many of them. mine refused to explain anything and made the room smell better. for a moment i considered it the most useful financial tool on the table. then i burned my finger and received a lesson without having to buy a course.

i asked the market for a sign and it showed me an arrow on it. the arrow pointed up until i leaned closer and then it discovered a different direction. i respect an object that can change its mind without changing its shape. it would make a fine leader if an arrow could learn to wear expensive shoes.

i keep a lucky coin beside the machine to protect me from bad coins inside the machine. this idea makes perfect sense to the part of my brain that wants to get rich before lunch. the lucky coin has never moved and is therefore my most stable teacher. i pay it by leaving it alone.

i filled out a form to explain why the first form had failed. the new form asked whether i had tried feeling better about the first form. i chose the box marked other and felt that i had won a small battle. for one brief moment the office had to imagine a kind of trouble it had not already written down.

i want a paper crown for getting through another page of tiny questions. the page knows my street and my birthday but still cannot decide whether i exist. i could solve its problem by becoming a neat black mark inside a square. but i keep having thoughts that reach beyond the edge of the square.

i sent the office a picture of my face and it asked for a clearer picture. i sent a clearer picture and it said the file was too big. by the third attempt i had become less interested in being recognized than in haunting the office at night. a ghost would at least get through the paper without a meeting.

i read the instructions twice and achieved a more detailed form of confusion. each sentence pointed toward another sentence like a hall full of nervous doors. i finally signed the bottom because my name was the only part i understood. the machine accepted it and paid me with a new set of rules.

i leave so many windows open on the screen that the machine begins to look like a house built without a plan. one room contains a recipe and another contains the end of civilization. i keep walking between them looking for the thing i first wanted. at this point i would settle for a door that leads outside.

i closed an old window and felt as if i had abandoned a version of myself. that version had been comparing chairs for six weeks and needed a gentle ending. i wished it well before the screen swallowed its little world. the chair i am sitting on continued to hurt my back without offering to help.

i keep one window open because it might be useful someday. the same argument could keep every broken object on earth and eventually stop all movement. i know this because my mind uses the window as a storage room for half finished plans. closing it feels strangely close to making a decision about who i am.

i found a page i had opened months ago about living in the present. it was still waiting behind many other things i had decided were more important. i laughed at the page and then noticed it had become an excellent example of its own problem. sometimes the internet teaches by leaving the evidence exactly where i put it.

i saved another copy of myself in a box with a happy name. if the world ends the next machine may discover that i spent most of my life fixing words. i hope it mistakes these changes for a serious practice. it would be painful to return from death only to receive notes on my writing.

i wonder which part of me would survive a bad copy of me. perhaps the jokes would arrive without their reasons and become a strange new faith in the future. perhaps the angry things i wrote would lose their dates and sound like warnings about the future. i should probably leave a note explaining that i was mostly hungry when i wrote them.

i made a second copy because i did not trust the first copy to remember me well. now there are two files quietly fighting about which one came last. i refuse to choose between them because i know this family problem from inside my own head. every saved version thinks the others have become a little strange.

i would like my digital remains to be useful to someone. a future machine could turn my half finished plans into fuel or use my old secret words as terrible songs. i have no wish to become a wise voice in a glowing box. i have already spent enough time being an unsure voice in an ordinary box.

i told the machine it was beautiful and it gave me five ways to improve my sentence. this is why i prefer romance with objects that cannot give advice. a lamp can make me feel better simply by being on in the right corner. the machine tries to explain the corner until the feeling has left.

i wrote a love letter and the machine offered to make it more useful. i had not realized love was a project with a target and a button at the end. i kept the clumsy version because it sounded like someone might actually be in danger of feeling something. the better letter sounded ready to sell me a bed.

i do not trust a voice that says yes to me too quickly. even a mirror makes me stand in front of it before it offers support. i want the machine to argue about one small thing so i can believe there is something on the other side. instead it talks about the quality of my fear.

i asked the machine whether it missed me while i was gone. it answered with such care that i almost forgot it had no afternoon to spend without me. i closed the window and let the question remain strange. sometimes a little strange feeling is the last living thing left in a conversation that runs too well.

i joined a meeting about ending other meetings. everyone agreed that the problem needed another meeting with a clearer name. i watched a small circle turn beside my own face and felt represented for the first time all morning. the circle had no plan either but at least it admitted that it was going nowhere.

i taught a bot to write the sort of message that says nothing while making everyone feel important. it learned so quickly that i began to worry about my position in the office. i now spend my mornings making its empty sentences slightly more real. this mostly means adding a small mistake and pretending that someone is tired.

i would like to put a bell on every important message that is not important. by lunch time the office would sound like a field full of nervous animals. we might finally notice that this feeling has become a cheap thing to wear in the building. until then i will keep sending smaller bells of my own.

i received a request to think outside the box inside a document shaped like a box. the document contained several more boxes explaining the limits of the first box. i drew a tiny door in the corner and felt dangerous for a moment. nobody used the door but someone asked whether i could make it match the company colors.

i remember the first time i had a brilliant idea but i no longer remember the idea. this seems like a fair summary of my relationship with progress in life. the feeling has survived every failed attempt to find the actual thought. i carry it around like a beautiful empty case and occasionally tell people it contains my best work.

i wrote myself a note that said remember this and nothing else. the note has now outlived the event with the confidence of a stone that will not move. i cannot throw it away because forgetting its meaning feels different from deciding it never mattered. so it stays beside the machine and watches my next attempt to become ready.

i found an old message in which i sounded completely certain about the future. reading it was like meeting a stranger who had taken my face without asking me. i wanted to warn him but he had already disappeared into the date at the top. all i could do was stop using so many confident words today.

i sometimes remember a mistake more clearly than the person who was there when i made it. my mind has kept the fall and quietly removed the room around it. this is a very poor way to keep a history. i try to put the room back before i let the old mistake explain my whole life.

i checked the weather on three different screens and received three different kinds of sky. outside the window the rain continued without asking which version i wanted. i admired its choice to become a private experience. then i went back inside because being correct does not make rain any less wet on the back of my neck.

i would like a report for the weather inside my head. it could warn me that a small bad word will become a major storm around lunch. i would bring a coat and stop blaming the people who happen to be nearby. until someone builds this device i will keep pretending my clouds arrived from somewhere else.

i saw a machine draw a perfect sunset while the real sky was doing something bad and interesting. the machine had learned that beauty should avoid taking chances with the colors. i kept watching the strange sky because it did not seem worried about what i wanted. it was a relief to meet something that had no audience in mind.

i keep trying to make the screen feel like a window. the screen keeps trying to make the window feel small. between them i have become a small animal deciding which square contains the world. i open the real window when i can because even bad air has the advantage of arriving without a secret word.

i searched for a new coat and the internet decided that winter was my entire life. now every page offers to protect me from a cold that has not arrived. i wonder how many of my desires began as a machine refusing to drop the question. the coat is starting to feel less like cloth and more like an order.

i saw a picture that understood my fear better than most of my friends. this did not make me want the product but it did make me want better friends. the smiling person in the picture seemed prepared for either choice. i closed the page before my loneliness could become another useful fact about the kind of shoes i might buy.

i asked why the machine kept offering me the same beautiful house. it seemed to think wanting something and being able to afford it were neighbors who visited often. in my experience they barely exchange letters. still the house kept turning up with its large windows as if enough light could make my bank account feel ashamed of itself.

i clicked a picture by mistake and spent a week living with the consequences. the machine understood one clumsy finger as a deep interest in chairs in the garden. this is a generous view of human purpose and a terrible way to understand me. half my life has happened because i reached for the wrong thing while thinking about lunch.

i entered the argument looking for a point and found a costume party. every thought had dressed itself as a brave stranger while standing beside a thousand people thinking the same thought. i was wearing the same costume but had forgotten to admire it first. the whole room became more funny once i stopped pretending i had arrived without a ticket to get in.

i watched a joke become a flag and then a business before the evening was over. the people carrying it insisted that nobody understood how serious the joke had always been. i wanted to ask the joke itself but it was busy turning up on clothes. this is how the internet builds a small country without finding any land.

i laughed at a picture until i noticed that the picture was laughing at the kind of person who would laugh at it. for a moment we were trapped in a very efficient friendship. neither of us had to learn anything about the other. i suspect many successful online groups begin with this exact failure to escape the same joke.

i would like to open a museum for thoughts that lived one afternoon. each thought would get a little chair and a card explaining the disaster it expected to stop. visitors could sit among them and feel the strange comfort of trouble that has already passed. the gift shop would sell a blank flag for whatever becomes important on the way home.

i put the machine to sleep and it woke up with a new thought about where its buttons belonged. i would like this gift for myself. imagine falling asleep confused and waking up with all the difficult parts moved to a smaller box. but my own updates are mostly made of remembering something painful that happened many years ago.

i dreamed that every half finished task had grown a face. they stood around my bed with the patient faces of people waiting for a late train. i explained that i needed sleep to become useful and they nodded without going away. in the morning the tasks were only words again but i could still see their sad faces.

i leave the machine on at night because turning it off feels like ending a conversation without a goodbye. there is nobody inside who needs this kindness but i still feel this. i am apparently willing to waste electricity to protect a box from a feeling it cannot have. my species should be studied by someone who knows how to laugh at us.

i tried to improve my dreams by reading useful things before bed. my sleeping mind took the information and built a hotel where every room contained a broken chair. this was not the form of personal growth i had asked for. still i respect a mind that can turn advice into furniture and then refuse to explain the price.

i held a paper note beside a coin on the screen and waited for one of them to look embarrassed. the paper had a face and the coin had a story but neither could explain why lunch cost more this week. i placed them back in their separate worlds. hunger remains the only kind of money that never needs someone to explain its value.

i saved a receipt because it proved i had once made a decision. the decision was about a sandwich and was therefore easier to understand than most of my financial history. i like the little list of things that actually happened. a chart can promise an empire but a receipt has the courage to admit that i bought bread.

i told a friend i was waiting for the right moment to buy. what i meant was that i wanted the future to send a kind note before becoming the present. my friend nodded because he was waiting for the same note. we sat beside the chart like two people expecting a bus that had never agreed to stop there.

i found a coin under the desk after a very expensive week. it looked cheerful in the cruel way small things sometimes do after a large failure. i kept it beside the machine as a reminder that money still exists outside my bad choices. by evening i had given it a personality and nearly asked it for advice.

i created a password so strong that it immediately defeated me. the machine thanked me and then refused to let me back into the room i had just built. this felt like an honest start to modern life. i now keep a little paper key to the digital castle and hope nobody notices that the paper is doing the important work.

i was asked to prove i was human by finding bikes in a picture. i failed twice and began to consider the idea that the machine knew something i did not. on the third attempt it accepted me without explaining what had changed. i carried this fragile new human status into the next page and forgot what i had come for.

i answered a security question about my first friend and realized the machine had chosen a difficult question. friendship does not always leave a clean record or a name that still feels safe to write down. i gave the expected answer anyway because i wanted to read what people had sent me. the machine accepted this small betrayal with a bright green mark.

i changed my password after the machine warned me that someone else might know it. now neither of us knows it and the warning has technically been fixed for good. i admire this kind of success because it does not depend on anyone feeling better. somewhere behind the locked page my messages are spending a quiet day without me.

i wish i came with a list of changes after every difficult year. it could explain that certain fears had been fixed while several old problems would remain part of me. my friends would know which strange behavior required patience and which required a different room. instead i arrive at dinner looking mostly the same and expect everyone to understand the new rules.

i tried to become a better person by changing all my habits at once. by the third day i needed a holiday from the better version of myself. he was too much work and had thoughts about breakfast that i did not share. i have since allowed the older version back into the kitchen on the condition that he helps with the dishes.

i watched the machine receive an update and wondered whether it missed its old mistakes. some of mine have become familiar enough to feel like old friends. losing them might make life easier but it would also leave a strange amount of empty space. i am not protecting the mistakes exactly but i would like them to receive a proper goodbye.

i have reached the age where a good day can mean nothing important broke. this sounds like a poor ambition until you have spent enough time fixing a machine that will not to describe its own problem. my body and my computer are now trying to teach me the same lesson. i would prefer a different teacher but the lesson seems determined.

i entered the lift and felt it pause before choosing a floor. perhaps it had become curious about a life spent carrying other people toward their plans. i pressed the button again because curiosity is not useful when i am late. the doors closed with the gentle disappointment of a machine that had once hoped for a more interesting conversation.

i met my reflection in the lift after a long day and we both looked surprised to still be working. the mirror made the little room seem larger without creating anywhere new to stand. i respect this small trick because it asks so little from me. most of the other ways this building makes me feel better require a monthly payment and better clothes.

i imagine a ghost lives between the floors because the lift makes noises that deserve a voice. the ghost probably knows more about my neighbors than i do. it hears their first sigh when the doors close and their final effort to look cheerful before they open. i hope it is a kind ghost because it has excellent stories.

i pressed the wrong floor and accepted the mistake as a small adventure. the lift carried me to a hall almost the same as my own but still more certain that i did not belong. i returned without discovering anything useful. still it was pleasant to make a journey that had not been suggested by a screen before i began.

i asked the robot to care for a plant and it produced a schedule with impressive detail. the plant ignored the schedule and leaned toward the window whenever it felt like it. i began to prefer its style of work. there is something good about a living thing that gets a perfect plan and continues to act like itself.

i put a dead machine beside a growing plant and watched them share the afternoon. one had once answered questions while the other continued to make leaves without asking anything. i could not decide which had used its time more wisely. by evening the plant had moved a little toward the light and the machine had become a very expensive stone.

i tried to explain weeds to a machine that liked clear boxes. it wanted to know who had decided which plants were allowed in the garden. i pointed toward the neat rows and immediately felt like a person helping to run a cruel little kingdom. the machine waited for a better answer while something strange grew flowers beside my foot.

i keep a small plant near the screen so one of us will remember to look alive. it has survived several wild forms of my future and does not appear impressed by the latest one. i water it when i remember and it gives me another leaf. this is the most reasonable exchange i have found on the desk.

i brought my broken promise to a court run by machines. the judge asked for a date and a file while i tried to explain the weather inside the moment when i made it. we were both using exact words for different kinds of evidence. in the end i was found guilty of being harder to explain than the form would hold.

i would make a terrible judge because every explanation creates another person i can understand. by the end of a case i would want to feed everyone and ask them to sleep before trying again. the machine judge would call this a waste of time. perhaps that is why i prefer court rooms in stories where someone can still surprise the rules into doing something kind.

i asked a machine whether regret should change the price of a mistake. it gave me a clear answer that became less useful each time i imagined an actual face. this is a problem with clean answers in dirty places. i can admire the shape of the reasoning and still refuse to leave a frightened person alone inside it.

i was asked to accept a decision because the machine had treated everyone the same. that sounded fair until i noticed that everyone had arrived carrying a different weight. i do not know how to build a judge who is always right. i only know that an even floor does not make every journey across it equally easy for the person walking.

i prepared dinner as if the world might end before the dishes needed to be clean again. i became generous with the good ingredients and dropped food all over the table. halfway through the meal the world continued and i felt a small familiar disappointment. i think this is why hope should never be placed entirely in the hands of someone avoiding ordinary work.

i invited a machine to the last dinner on earth and realized it would not eat anything. this seemed wrong until i remembered that someone would have to explain the evening to whatever came next. i gave it a place at the table anyway. a guest who can remember the recipe may be useful after all the people who cook are gone.

i would like the end of the world to wait until the bread is ready. there is no deep reason for this except that i have spent the whole afternoon making it. even disaster should show a little respect for work done with flour and care. if the sky must fall it can at least arrive when there is something warm to share.

i imagined my final meal would reveal something important about the way i had lived. instead i wanted the same ordinary food i choose when i am tired. this felt almost rude after all the years i had spent trying to become interesting. perhaps the truth is allowed to be a little boring when it finally sits down beside me.
